blocks.text: Silent killers underground: the urgent threat of plant-parasitic nematodes

blocks.body: Plant-parasitic nematodes (PPNs) are among the most destructive pathogens in global agricultural production. Widely distributed in cultivated soils, they parasitize plant roots, disrupt nutrient uptake pathways and trigger secondary diseases, posing severe threats to crop yield and quality. Statistically, PPNs cause up to 157 billion dollars in annual crop losses worldwide across more than 20 major cash crops[1]. Among them, sedentary endoparasitic nematodes represent the most harmful group due to their unique parasitic lifestyle, strong dispersal capacity and difficult control[2]. As two representative species, Heterodera glycines and Meloidogyne incognita exhibit typical taxonomic and biological features. They continuously endanger the production of globally critical crops and serve as core model organisms for research on soil nematode management (Figure 1).

blocks.alt: Symptoms of two major plant-parasitic nematodes on soybean roots. (a) Meloidogyne incognita: obvious root galls formed on infected soybean roots. (b) Heterodera glycines: white lemon-shaped mature females protruding from soybean roots (arrows). Note that soybean cyst nematode does not form root galls.
blocks.body: Figure 1. Symptoms of two major PPNs on soybean roots. (a) M. incognita: obvious root galls formed on infected soybean roots. (b) H. glycines: white lemon-shaped mature females protruding from soybean roots (arrows). Note that soybean cyst nematode does not form root galls. Source: Management of Plant-Parasitic Nematodes in Florida Soybean Production (NG018), UF/IFAS EDIS. Used for educational demonstration only.

PPNs of these two species exert substantial economic and ecological impacts. H. glycines specifically parasitizes legumes such as soybean and common bean. After second-stage juveniles invade host roots, they secrete effectors to induce syncytial feeding sites, which leads to root lignification, stunting and chlorosis of plants. In heavily infested fields, soybean yield losses can reach 30%–80% or even total crop failure. The cysts of this nematode can remain dormant in soil for more than 10 years, serving as persistent primary inoculum sources that are hard to eradicate, making it the most devastating disease in major soybean-producing regions worldwide[3].

As a polyphagous sedentary endoparasitic nematode, M. incognita infects over 3000 plant species including vegetables, grain and cash crops such as tomato, cucumber, cotton and maize[1]. Losses caused by this nematode are especially severe in protected agriculture due to continuous cropping obstacles. Notably, M. incognita secretes secondary metabolites such as 6-methoxybenzoxazolin-2-one to modulate the rhizosphere microbiome, improving its host-finding capacity and further expanding its damage range[4].

Co-infection by these two nematodes elevates the risk of complex soil-borne disease outbreaks and creates a “dual stress” on crop production. Therefore, systematic identification of detection and control targets for the two nematodes will not only enrich nematode management tools, but also provide universal strategies for eco-friendly control of nematode diseases in global agriculture.

blocks.text: Control dilemma: the critical weakness of current nematode control systems
blocks.attributes: #control-dilemma toc="Control dilemma: the critical weakness of current nematode control systems"

blocks.body: Current major management strategies for nematode diseases include chemical fumigation, non-fumigant nematicides, novel nematicides, biological control, resistant cultivar breeding, and crop rotation. To maximize the efficacy of these control approaches while lowering their environmental risks, multiple detection technologies for PPNs have been developed[5]. Nevertheless, these methods generally suffer from delayed detection, high cost, poor portability, and heavy reliance on professional operators (Table 1).

blocks.text: Dawn breaks: nematophagous fungi fuel innovation in nematode detection

blocks.body: Previous studies revealed that ascaroside #18 (ascr#18) acts as the dominant ascaroside across multiple genera of PPNs (Figure 2)[6]. In contrast, larvae of free-living nematodes such as Caenorhabditis elegans mainly produce ascaroside #3 (ascr#3) and ascaroside #5 (ascr#5) (Figure 3)[7].
Figure 2. Ascaroside profiles in PPNs. Source: Manosalva P, et al. (2015), Nature Communications, DOI:10.1038/ncomms8795.
Figure 3. Ascaroside profiles in free-living nematodes. Source: Lee D, et al. (2023), Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, DOI:10.1073/pnas.2221150120.

Recent studies demonstrate that the G protein-coupled receptor GPR2 from the nematode-trapping fungus Arthrobotrys oligospora can sense ascr#3. It triggers a mitogen-activated protein kinase cascade to activate downstream gene expression and ultimately initiate predatory behavior (Figure 4) [8]. This inspired our idea: we could repurpose this receptor to achieve early warning of PPNs!
